questions.stem: An 84 year old woman is admitted with 4 days of cough and poor oral intake. She has passed little urine today. Her mucous membranes are dry. Her temperature is 38.3°C, pulse rate 112 bpm, BP 94/58 mmHg and respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute. Her creatinine three months ago was 82 µmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Dehydration and sepsis reduce renal perfusion; concentrated urine (osmolality over 500 mOsm/kg) and a disproportionate rise in urea point to pre-renal AKI, the commonest type. ATN gives dilute urine with high sodium.

steps.x: Sepsis and dehydration with hypotension, urea rising more than creatinine and concentrated urine.

elim: Drug-induced, often with rash and eosinophilia; urine would not be concentrated.
Gives dilute urine with a high urinary sodium.
Her creatinine was normal three months ago.
No retention, palpable bladder or obstructive history.

steps.x: E: Pre-renal acute kidney injury. Hypoperfusion + concentrated urine (>500 mOsm/kg) + urea rising more than creatinine = pre-renal.

questions.stem: A 71 year old man had an open repair of a ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm 2 days ago and was hypotensive for over an hour during surgery. His urine output has been 10 mL/h for 18 hours and did not improve after a 1 litre fluid challenge. He is now euvolaemic. His BP is 128/72 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his acute kidney injury?
questions.e: Prolonged hypotension causes ischaemic acute tubular necrosis; damaged tubules cannot reabsorb sodium, giving high urinary sodium, FeNa over 1% and dilute urine, with no response to fluids. Pre-renal AKI would improve with fluids.

clues: did not improve after a 1 litre fluid challenge
steps.x: Prolonged hypotension, no response to fluid, high urinary sodium and FeNa, dilute urine.

elim: Gives haematuria and proteinuria with red cell casts, not a link to hypotension.
No hydronephrosis was suggested and urine sodium fits tubular injury.
Would respond to fluid and give concentrated urine with low sodium.
A chronic cause unmasked by ACE inhibitors, not hypotension-induced injury.

steps.x: B: Acute tubular necrosis. Intrinsic AKI (ATN): FeNa >1%, high urine sodium, osmolality <350, poor response to a fluid challenge.

questions.stem: A 58 year old man has a CT coronary angiogram with iodinated contrast. He has type 2 diabetes and takes naproxen for knee pain. Three days later his creatinine has risen from 98 to 260 µmol/L. He is euvolaemic and his bladder is not palpable. A urine sample is sent for microscopy.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on urine microscopy?
questions.e: Contrast and NSAIDs are nephrotoxins that cause acute tubular necrosis; sloughed tubular cells form muddy brown granular casts. Red cell casts point to glomerulonephritis.

steps.x: Nephrotoxins (contrast and an NSAID) in a euvolaemic patient: ATN.

elim: Seen in concentrated urine in pre-renal states.
Suggest glomerulonephritis.
Suggest tumour lysis or urate nephropathy.
Suggest pyelonephritis or interstitial nephritis.

steps.x: B: Muddy brown granular casts. Sloughed tubular cells in ATN form muddy brown casts.

questions.stem: A 52 year old woman with advanced cervical cancer has 3 days of reduced urine output and nausea. Her creatinine has risen from 70 to 390 µmol/L over a week. Her pulse rate is 84 bpm and BP 136/80 mmHg, and her bladder is not palpable. Ultrasound shows bilateral hydronephrosis with an empty bladder.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her acute kidney injury?
questions.e: Post-renal AKI is caused by obstruction, here bilateral ureteric compression by pelvic tumour; the empty bladder shows the block is above it. Bladder outlet obstruction would give a full bladder.

clues: bilateral hydronephrosis with an empty bladder
steps.x: Pelvic tumour with bilateral hydronephrosis and an empty bladder.

elim: Would not cause bilateral hydronephrosis.
The bladder is empty, so the block is above it.
She is not dry or hypotensive, and it would not cause hydronephrosis.
Does not cause bilateral hydronephrosis.

steps.x: B: Bilateral ureteric obstruction by tumour. Post-renal AKI: obstruction from BPH, stones or tumours; an empty bladder places the block at the ureters.

questions.stem: An 88 year old man in a care home has become confused over 2 days and is restless and in pain. Staff say he has been dribbling small amounts of urine. He takes oxybutynin, recently started for urgency. His pulse rate is 96 bpm and BP 154/88 mmHg. His creatinine has risen from 104 to 286 µmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on abdominal examination?
o: Pulsatile, expansile mass above the umbilicus
questions.e: Anticholinergics such as oxybutynin can precipitate retention in older men; post-renal AKI from retention presents with confusion, suprapubic pain and a palpable bladder.

steps.x: Anticholinergic drug, overflow dribbling, pain and confusion: retention.

elim: Suggests a renal mass or polycystic kidney, not acute retention.
An abdominal aortic aneurysm.
Ascites.
Suggests appendicitis or other bowel pathology.

steps.x: B: Dull, tender suprapubic mass. Post-renal AKI from retention gives a palpable, dull, tender bladder.

questions.stem: A 69 year old man with heart failure takes ramipril and furosemide. For 2 weeks he has been taking over-the-counter tablets for gout in his big toe. He feels nauseated and tired. His creatinine has risen from 110 to 248 µmol/L. He is euvolaemic and his bladder is not palpable.
questions.q: Which is the most likely precipitant of his acute kidney injury?
questions.e: NSAIDs such as ibuprofen are common precipitants of AKI, especially with an ACE inhibitor and a diuretic ('triple whammy'), which together remove the kidney's ability to maintain GFR.

steps.x: ACE inhibitor + diuretic + a new over-the-counter painkiller.

elim: Not used for acute gout or sold over the counter; it is not the classic culprit here.
Prescription-only; toxicity causes diarrhoea rather than this classic drug combination.
Not nephrotoxic at normal doses.
Not nephrotoxic and not bought over the counter.

steps.x: C: Ibuprofen. NSAID + ACE inhibitor + diuretic is the 'triple whammy' that precipitates AKI.

questions.stem: A 79 year old woman with CKD stage 3a is treated by her GP for a urinary tract infection. Five days later routine bloods show her creatinine has risen from 120 to 168 µmol/L and her potassium is 5.8 mmol/L. She is well hydrated. She takes amlodipine and atorvastatin, which are unchanged.
questions.q: Which drug is most likely to be responsible?
questions.e: Trimethoprim is a recognised precipitant of AKI and hyperkalaemia, as it blocks tubular creatinine secretion and potassium excretion; underlying CKD increases the risk. Nitrofurantoin and the penicillins rarely do this.

steps.x: A UTI antibiotic followed by a rise in creatinine and potassium.

elim: Not usually linked to a rise in creatinine and potassium.
Rarely affects creatinine or potassium.
A single-dose treatment not linked to this picture.
Not linked to a rise in creatinine and potassium.

steps.x: E: Trimethoprim. Trimethoprim is a less common but classic precipitant: raises creatinine and potassium.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man with CKD stage 3b is admitted with a stroke. He has an MRI brain with an intravenous contrast agent to look for a tumour. Four days later his creatinine has risen from 150 to 240 µmol/L. He has been eating and drinking well and his BP has been stable. No new drugs have been started.
questions.q: Which is the most likely precipitant of his acute kidney injury?
questions.e: MRI contrast agents such as gadolinium are a less common precipitant of AKI, and pre-existing CKD increases the risk; there is no sign of dehydration or obstruction.

clues: MRI brain with an intravenous contrast agent
steps.x: Underlying CKD with recent MRI contrast and no other cause.

elim: Cardioprotective-dose aspirin is not a significant nephrotoxin.
He has been eating and drinking well with stable BP.
Does not directly cause AKI.
Nothing suggests retention.

steps.x: C: Gadolinium contrast. MRI contrast agents such as gadolinium are a less common cause; CKD is a risk factor.

questions.stem: A 63 year old man is found to have a creatinine of 380 µmol/L at a new GP registration. He has no previous blood results. He has had tiredness and itching for months. His BP is 168/96 mmHg. The doctor wants to know whether this is acute kidney injury.
questions.q: Which result most suggests that the kidney disease is chronic rather than acute?
questions.e: Hypocalcaemia suggests the kidney disease is chronic, reflecting long-standing loss of vitamin D activation; high potassium, urea and acidosis occur in both acute and chronic disease.

steps.x: No baseline, so look for markers of long-standing disease.

elim: Occurs in both acute and chronic disease.
Occurs in both acute and chronic disease.
Metabolic acidosis occurs in both.
Points to inflammation or infection, not chronicity.

steps.x: C: Low adjusted calcium. Hypocalcaemia suggests chronic rather than acute kidney disease (reduced vitamin D activation over time).

questions.stem: A 44 year old man takes simvastatin 80 mg and was started on clarithromycin for a chest infection 5 days ago. He now has aching, weak thighs and his urine is the colour of cola. His creatinine is 310 µmol/L, from 85 µmol/L last month. Urine dipstick is strongly positive for blood but microscopy shows no red cells.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his acute kidney injury?
questions.e: Clarithromycin raises simvastatin levels, causing rhabdomyolysis; myoglobin gives dark urine and a positive dipstick without red cells, and damages the tubules. CK is raised and rapid IV fluids are needed.

steps.x: Statin plus a CYP3A4 inhibitor, myalgia, dark urine, dipstick blood without red cells (myoglobin).

elim: Does not cause myalgia and dipstick blood without red cells.
Follows bloody diarrhoea with anaemia and low platelets.
Causes visible haematuria with red cells, not myalgia.
Cause colicky loin pain and red cells in the urine.

steps.x: E: Rhabdomyolysis. Rhabdomyolysis: myoglobin injures tubules; check CK and give rapid IV fluids.

questions.stem: A 67 year old man has had oliguric acute kidney injury for 6 days. He now has central chest pain that is better when he sits forward. A scratchy sound is heard over the left sternal edge. His urea is 46 mmol/L and creatinine 820 µmol/L. ECG shows widespread saddle-shaped ST elevation.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his chest pain?
questions.e: Severe uraemia causes pericarditis (pain relieved by sitting forward, a rub, saddle ST elevation), which is an indication for urgent dialysis. MI gives territorial ST elevation.

steps.x: Positional chest pain with a rub and saddle ST elevation in severe uraemia.

elim: ST elevation would be in one territory with reciprocal change, and pain is not positional.
Tearing pain to the back, not positional pain with a rub.
Pleuritic pain with hypoxia, not a pericardial rub.
Possible, but the very high urea makes uraemia the cause.

steps.x: D: Uraemic pericarditis. Pericarditis in AKI = severe uraemia = an indication for dialysis.

questions.stem: An 80 kg man is on the surgical ward 2 days after a hip replacement. His creatinine is unchanged from baseline. The nurse records his hourly urine output on a fluid balance chart. The doctor wants to know when urine output alone would meet the criterion for acute kidney injury.
questions.q: Which urine output meets the criterion for acute kidney injury?
questions.e: AKI is defined by urine output below 0.5 mL/kg/h for more than 6 hours; for 80 kg that is under 40 mL/h, so 30 mL/h for 7 hours qualifies. 35 mL/h for 4 hours is too short.

steps.x: 80 kg, so 0.5 mL/kg/h = 40 mL/h.

elim: Below 0.5 mL/kg/h (40 mL/h) but for less than 6 hours.
Above 0.5 mL/kg/h (40 mL/h).
Above 0.5 mL/kg/h.
Normal output.

steps.x: A: 30 mL/h for 7 hours. AKI by urine output: below 0.5 mL/kg/h for more than 6 hours.

questions.stem: A 76 year old woman has oliguric acute kidney injury after a week of diarrhoea. She takes spironolactone and ramipril for heart failure. She feels weak and has palpitations. Her potassium is 7.4 mmol/L (3.5–5.3) and creatinine 410 µmol/L. A 12-lead ECG is recorded.
questions.q: Which is the most likely ECG finding?
o: ST elevation in V1 to V4
questions.e: The kidney is the main route of potassium excretion, so AKI (worsened by spironolactone and ramipril) causes hyperkalaemia; membrane depolarisation gives tall tented T waves and risks fatal arrhythmia. U waves suggest hypokalaemia.

steps.x: Severe hyperkalaemia from AKI plus potassium-retaining drugs.

elim: Seen in Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome.
Seen in hypokalaemia.
Not a feature of hyperkalaemia, which lengthens the PR.
Suggests anterior myocardial infarction.

steps.x: B: Peaked (tented) T waves. The kidney excretes most potassium; hyperkalaemia gives tented T waves and risks fatal arrhythmia.

questions.stem: A 61 year old man has had 2 days of black, tarry stools. He takes naproxen for back pain. He is pale and clammy. His pulse rate is 124 bpm and BP 86/50 mmHg. His haemoglobin is 72 g/L. His urea is 24.8 mmol/L and creatinine 142 µmol/L (baseline 90 µmol/L).
questions.q: Which is the most likely type of acute kidney injury?
questions.e: Blood loss from an upper GI bleed causes hypovolaemic shock and reduced renal perfusion: pre-renal AKI, with urea rising far more than creatinine. ATN can follow if hypoperfusion persists.

steps.x: Blood loss with shock and urea rising far more than creatinine.

elim: Would cause haematuria and proteinuria, not hypovolaemic shock.
Possible with NSAIDs but would not explain the shock and high urea.
Can follow if hypoperfusion persists; it is not the first picture here.
No obstruction is suggested.

steps.x: E: Pre-renal acute kidney injury. Pre-renal causes include blood loss; upper GI bleeding also raises urea (digested blood).

questions.stem: A 74 year old woman is listed for an elective open bowel resection. Her surgeon assesses her risk of acute kidney injury after surgery. She has hypertension controlled with amlodipine, a BMI of 29 kg/m², and an eGFR of 34 mL/min/1.73m² that has been stable for 3 years.
questions.q: Which feature puts her at greatest risk of acute kidney injury after surgery?
questions.e: CKD is the strongest risk factor for AKI, and major surgery is a common precipitant; amlodipine is not nephrotoxic.

steps.x: Stable reduced eGFR before major surgery.

elim: A risk factor, but less important than reduced baseline kidney function.
Not nephrotoxic.
Not a major AKI risk factor.
Not a major AKI risk factor.

steps.x: D: Chronic kidney disease. CKD and surgery are both common precipitants of AKI.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man is admitted with cellulitis. His creatinine on admission is 84 µmol/L. He is given intravenous flucloxacillin and fluids. The team check his U&Es daily and his urine output on a fluid balance chart.
questions.q: Which result meets the criteria for acute kidney injury?
questions.e: AKI is diagnosed by a creatinine rise of 26 µmol/L or more within 48 hours (here 32 in 24 hours), a rise of 50% or more within 7 days, or urine output under 0.5 mL/kg/h for over 6 hours.

steps.x: Baseline creatinine 84 µmol/L.

elim: A rise of only 14 µmol/L, under 26 µmol/L.
A 24% rise, under 50% in 7 days.
Urea alone does not define AKI.
Above 0.5 mL/kg/h.

steps.x: B: Creatinine 116 µmol/L 24 hours after admission. AKI: creatinine rise of 26 µmol/L or more in 48 hours, or 50% or more in 7 days, or UO <0.5 mL/kg/h for >6 h.

questions.stem: A 63 year old woman is treated for pyelonephritis. Her baseline creatinine is 90 µmol/L. Five days into admission it is 205 µmol/L. Her urine output has been 0.4 mL/kg/h for the last 8 hours. She is not anuric.

visual.title: Creatinine as multiple of baseline
visual.label: 2.3x
visual.caption: Creatinine 205 µmol/L against a baseline of 90.

questions.q: Which is the stage of her acute kidney injury?
questions.e: Creatinine 2.3 times baseline is stage 2 (2 to 2.99 times); the urine output criterion only reaches stage 1, and the highest stage is used.

steps.x: 205/90 = 2.3 times baseline; urine output criterion = stage 1.

elim: Her creatinine has more than doubled.
Her urine output meets stage 1, but creatinine meets a higher stage.
Creatinine is not 3 times baseline or over 354 µmol/L.
AKI is staged 1 to 3 only.

steps.x: C: Stage 2. Stage by whichever criterion gives the highest stage: 2 to 2.99 times baseline = stage 2.

questions.stem: A 57 year old man on ICU with severe pancreatitis has a creatinine of 150 µmol/L from a baseline of 92 µmol/L 3 days ago. He has passed no urine through his catheter for the last 13 hours, and the catheter has been flushed and is not blocked.
questions.q: Which is the stage of his acute kidney injury?
o: Stage 3 only if dialysis is started
questions.e: AKI is staged by whichever criterion gives the highest stage; creatinine 1.6 times baseline is stage 1, but anuria for 12 hours or more is stage 3.

steps.x: Creatinine 1.6 times baseline, but anuric for 13 hours.

elim: Both creatinine and urine output criteria are met.
Creatinine (1.6 times baseline) gives stage 1, but anuria gives a higher stage.
Would need 2 to 2.99 times baseline or oliguria over 12 hours, but anuria for 12 hours is stage 3.
Dialysis is not needed for stage 3; anuria for 12 hours is enough.

steps.x: D: Stage 3. Use the criterion giving the highest stage; anuria for 12 hours = stage 3.

questions.stem: A 78 year old woman has had 3 days of vomiting and feels dizzy on standing. She takes bendroflumethiazide and ramipril. Her mucous membranes are dry. Her pulse rate is 104 bpm and BP 102/60 mmHg lying and 82/50 mmHg standing.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
o: CT of the kidneys, ureters and bladder
questions.e: U&Es are the first-line test for suspected AKI, showing a rising creatinine plus sodium and potassium disturbances; ultrasound comes next if the cause is unclear.

steps.x: Dehydration on a diuretic and ACE inhibitor: possible AKI and electrolyte disturbance.

elim: For suspected stones; not the first test.
A specialist test of split renal function.
For unexplained intrinsic disease, not first-line.
Used for unexplained AKI to exclude obstruction, after U&Es.

steps.x: E: Urea and electrolytes. U&Es first-line, showing a rising creatinine and the potassium and sodium.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man with acute kidney injury from sepsis becomes breathless. He is breathing deeply and rapidly. His chest is clear on auscultation. His oxygen saturation is 98% breathing air, pulse rate 102 bpm and BP 118/70 mmHg. His creatinine is 520 µmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next bedside investigation?
questions.e: Deep, rapid (Kussmaul) breathing with a clear chest and normal saturation suggests metabolic acidosis in severe AKI; a blood gas confirms pH, bicarbonate and potassium. A pH under 7.20 is an indication for dialysis.

steps.x: Kussmaul breathing in severe AKI: metabolic acidosis.

elim: His chest is clear and he is not hypoxic.
Not suggested by deep breathing with normal saturation in AKI.
For asthma, which this is not.
Helps find the cause but not this breathlessness.

steps.x: E: Venous blood gas. Blood gas is a key bedside test in AKI to find acidosis and check potassium.

questions.stem: A 72 year old man has a creatinine of 312 µmol/L, from 96 µmol/L six weeks ago. He has no vomiting, diarrhoea or new drugs and his BP is 142/84 mmHg. He has had poor urine stream for 2 years. His bladder is not obviously palpable because of his body habitus.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation within 24 hours?
questions.e: Renal tract ultrasound within 24 hours is first-line for unexplained AKI, to look for obstruction such as hydronephrosis from BPH. Biopsy comes only once obstruction is excluded.

clues: no vomiting, diarrhoea or new drugs
steps.x: Unexplained AKI with prostatic symptoms.

elim: Not first-line for AKI.
Not relevant.
Only after obstruction is excluded and intrinsic disease suspected.
Gadolinium is a risk in AKI and this is not first-line.

steps.x: E: Renal tract ultrasound. Unexplained AKI: renal tract ultrasound within 24 hours to exclude obstruction.

questions.stem: A 49 year old woman is admitted with acute kidney injury. Her creatinine is 240 µmol/L from 70 µmol/L last month. Her BP is 156/94 mmHg. She has ankle swelling but no lung crackles. She takes no regular drugs and her bladder is not palpable. The doctor wants a quick bedside test to point to the type of AKI.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial bedside test?
questions.e: Urine dipstick is a quick bedside test that helps distinguish pre-renal, intrinsic and post-renal AKI; blood and protein suggest a glomerular cause needing a renal screen.

steps.x: AKI of unclear type, possibly glomerular.

elim: Not indicated without fever.
Useful generally, but does not point to the type of AKI.
Assesses postural drop, not the site of kidney injury.
Not relevant.

steps.x: E: Urine dipstick. Urine dipstick helps distinguish pre-renal, intrinsic and post-renal causes (blood and protein suggest glomerular disease).

questions.stem: A 26 year old woman has 2 months of painful joints, mouth ulcers and a rash over her cheeks that spares the nasolabial folds. Her creatinine has risen from 68 to 190 µmol/L over 3 weeks. Urine dipstick shows blood +++ and protein +++. Her BP is 150/96 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to identify the cause?
o: ANA, anti-dsDNA and complement (C3 and C4)
questions.e: Intrinsic glomerular AKI needs a renal screen; with features of lupus, ANA, anti-dsDNA and low complement (C3 and C4) point to lupus nephritis. Anti-GBM is for pulmonary-renal syndrome.

steps.x: Young woman with SLE features and a glomerular urine dipstick.

elim: For Goodpasture's disease with lung haemorrhage, not a malar rash and arthritis.
For rhabdomyolysis.
Not relevant in a woman.
For gout or urate nephropathy, not this picture.

steps.x: A: ANA, anti-dsDNA and complement (C3 and C4). Suspected glomerular cause: renal screen including ANA, dsDNA, C3, C4, ANCA, anti-GBM, electrophoresis.

questions.stem: A 77 year old man is admitted with acute kidney injury after 4 days of diarrhoea. His creatinine has risen from 95 to 260 µmol/L. He has type 2 diabetes, heart failure and a metallic mitral valve. His drug list includes metformin, furosemide, ramipril, naproxen and warfarin.
questions.q: Which drug is most appropriate to continue?
questions.e: Stop nephrotoxic and risky drugs using DAMN: diuretics, ACE inhibitors, metformin and NSAIDs. Warfarin is considered safe to continue, especially with a metallic valve, with INR monitoring.

clues: metformin, furosemide, ramipril, naproxen and warfarin
steps.x: Dehydration AKI with several drugs to review.

elim: A diuretic; worsens dehydration and should be withheld.
Risk of toxicity (lactic acidosis) in AKI; withhold.
An NSAID; nephrotoxic, stop.
An ACE inhibitor; withhold in AKI.

steps.x: E: Warfarin. DAMN: stop Diuretics, ACE inhibitors/ARBs, Metformin, NSAIDs; warfarin is safe to continue (monitor INR).

questions.stem: A 54 year old woman with bipolar disorder has taken lithium for 12 years. She has had 3 days of vomiting and now has a coarse tremor and is unsteady on her feet. Her creatinine has risen from 80 to 190 µmol/L. Her pulse rate is 98 bpm and BP 108/66 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate immediate step in management of her medication?
o: Continue lithium and add sodium valproate
Continue lithium at the same dose
Hold lithium and check a lithium level
Switch lithium to a once-weekly dose
questions.e: Lithium is renally excreted, so AKI raises its level and toxicity risk; a coarse tremor and ataxia suggest toxicity. Withhold it, check a level and rehydrate.

steps.x: AKI from vomiting with signs of lithium toxicity.

elim: Lithium must be stopped first.
Lithium accumulates in AKI and is toxic.
Would worsen toxicity.
Not a safe option; lithium should be stopped.

steps.x: D: Hold lithium and check a lithium level. Lithium has increased toxicity risk in AKI: withhold and check levels.

questions.stem: A 70 year old woman with acute kidney injury from pneumonia has received 5 litres of intravenous fluid in 48 hours. She is now breathless, with bilateral leg oedema, a raised JVP and crackles at both lung bases. Her urine output is 40 mL/h. Her oxygen saturation is 91% breathing air and BP 148/88 mmHg. Potassium is 5.0 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Give a further 500 mL bolus of 0.9% sodium chloride
Insert a urinary catheter for retention
questions.e: Fluid overload in AKI shows as oedema and crackles; stop fluids and give a loop diuretic such as furosemide if she is still passing urine. Refractory pulmonary oedema is an indication for dialysis.

steps.x: Fluid overload with oedema and crackles, still passing urine.

elim: She is overloaded; more fluid worsens pulmonary oedema.
Her potassium is normal.
She is passing 40 mL/h.
An ACE inhibitor should be withheld in AKI.

steps.x: D: Intravenous furosemide and stop fluids. Assess fluid status: fluids if dry, diuretics if overloaded.

questions.stem: An 81 year old man has not passed urine for 12 hours and has severe lower abdominal pain. He has had nocturia and hesitancy for 2 years. There is a tender, dull mass rising out of the pelvis. His creatinine has risen from 102 to 240 µmol/L. His pulse rate is 98 bpm and BP 162/90 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Catheterise the bladder and give paracetamol
Renal tract ultrasound before any treatment
Transurethral resection of the prostate today
questions.e: Post-renal AKI from BPH is treated by urethral catheterisation, which relieves the obstruction and restores filtration, with paracetamol for pain. Fluids do not treat obstruction.

steps.x: Acute retention from BPH causing post-renal AKI.

elim: He is not dry; the problem is obstruction.
Takes time and does not relieve acute retention now.
Delays relief of painful retention.
Not the emergency treatment.

steps.x: A: Catheterise the bladder and give paracetamol. Post-renal: catheterisation plus analgesia (paracetamol) relieves obstruction and restores flow.

questions.stem: A 68 year old woman is 12 hours after an elective right hemicolectomy. Her urine output has been 20 mL/h for 4 hours (she weighs 70 kg). Her pulse rate is 104 bpm, BP 104/64 mmHg and capillary refill time 3 seconds. Her abdomen is soft, the drain contains little blood and her haemoglobin is unchanged. Her chest is clear.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Intravenous fluid challenge of 500 mL crystalloid
questions.e: Post-operative urine output under 0.5 mL/kg/h without haemorrhage or fluid overload should first be treated with a fluid challenge. Furosemide would worsen pre-renal hypoperfusion.

steps.x: Post-operative oliguria with mild tachycardia and no bleeding or overload.

elim: She is under-filled; a diuretic would worsen perfusion.
No indication; first try to restore perfusion.
No signs of haemorrhage or leak.
Not indicated in post-operative oliguria.

steps.x: A: Intravenous fluid challenge of 500 mL crystalloid. Post-op UO <0.5 mL/kg/h: first consider a fluid challenge if no contraindication or haemorrhage.

questions.stem: A 72 year old man with acute kidney injury has a potassium of 7.1 mmol/L (3.5–5.3). He feels weak. His pulse rate is 64 bpm and BP 132/78 mmHg. His ECG is shown (see item resources).

visual.title: 12-lead ECG
visual.caption: Tall tented T waves across the chest and inferior leads.

questions.q: Which is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
o: Stop ramipril and recheck in 24 hours
questions.e: Hyperkalaemia with tented T waves risks a fatal arrhythmia; IV calcium gluconate stabilises the cardiac membrane immediately, before treatments that shift or remove potassium.

steps.x: Severe hyperkalaemia with ECG changes.

elim: Does not protect the heart from hyperkalaemia.
Too slow and unreliable to lower potassium.
Acts over hours; does not protect the heart now.
Leaves him at immediate risk of a fatal arrhythmia.

steps.x: B: Intravenous calcium gluconate. Hyperkalaemia with ECG changes: IV calcium gluconate first to stabilise the myocardium.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man has oliguric acute kidney injury from sepsis. Despite fluids and stopping nephrotoxic drugs he remains acidotic on repeat testing. His potassium is 5.9 mmol/L. His chest is clear and his urea is 28 mmol/L with no confusion or pericardial rub.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Continue current management and recheck in 24 hours
questions.e: Severe metabolic acidosis with pH under 7.20 despite treatment is an AEIOU indication for renal replacement therapy (dialysis or haemofiltration).

steps.x: Severe refractory metabolic acidosis (pH 7.12).

elim: pH under 7.20 is an indication for dialysis now.
His potassium is not severely high and there are no ECG changes.
He is not overloaded and it will not correct the acidosis.
Too slow for severe refractory acidosis.

steps.x: B: Dialysis (renal replacement therapy). AEIOU: Acidosis (pH <7.20), Electrolytes (K >7), Intoxication, Overload, Uraemia.

questions.stem: A 58 year old woman has AKI from acute tubular necrosis after cardiac surgery. She has passed 80 mL of urine in 24 hours. She is breathless with crackles to the mid-zones despite high-dose intravenous furosemide and oxygen. Her oxygen saturation is 89% on 40% oxygen and BP 142/84 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: A further dose of intravenous furosemide
questions.e: Pulmonary oedema refractory to diuretics is an AEIOU indication (Overload) for renal replacement therapy such as haemofiltration; persistent potassium over 7 mmol/L is another.

clues: crackles to the mid-zones despite high-dose intravenous furosemide
steps.x: Refractory pulmonary oedema in near-anuric AKI.

elim: She has already failed high-dose diuretics.
Would worsen pulmonary oedema.
Too slow and raises potassium.
Would worsen AKI and does not treat pulmonary oedema.

steps.x: B: Haemofiltration. Refractory fluid overload (O in AEIOU) = haemofiltration.

questions.stem: A 79 year old woman is admitted with stage 2 acute kidney injury after gastroenteritis. She is given intravenous fluids and her ramipril and furosemide are withheld. Her pulse rate is now 86 bpm and BP 124/72 mmHg. The nurse asks how she should be monitored.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate monitoring?
o: Daily U&Es and a fluid balance chart with urine output
questions.e: In AKI, U&Es and urine output are monitored regularly (daily bloods and a fluid balance chart) to track recovery and catch hyperkalaemia, fluid overload, acidosis and uraemia.

steps.x: Active AKI on IV fluids.

elim: Does not track kidney recovery, potassium or fluid status.
Too infrequent in active AKI.
Too infrequent and misses potassium.
Too infrequent; eGFR is not valid in AKI.

steps.x: B: Daily U&Es and a fluid balance chart with urine output. Monitor U&Es and urine output regularly: watch for hyperkalaemia, overload, acidosis and uraemia.

questions.stem: A 67 year old man with hypertension and diabetic kidney disease starts ramipril. His creatinine before starting was 110 µmol/L. Two weeks later it is 132 µmol/L and his potassium is 5.1 mmol/L. He feels well and his BP has fallen from 158/92 to 140/84 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.e: A small creatinine rise is expected with ACE inhibitors because they reduce efferent arteriolar tone; a rise under 30% (here 20%) means continue with monitoring, whereas over 30% means stop.

steps.x: A 20% creatinine rise 2 weeks after starting an ACE inhibitor.

elim: Would raise potassium further and is not indicated.
A 20% rise does not suggest renal artery stenosis.
He is well and not dehydrated.
Only needed if creatinine rises by more than 30%.

steps.x: B: Continue ramipril and recheck U&Es. Stop the ACE inhibitor if creatinine rises over 30% from baseline after 2 weeks; under that, continue and monitor.

questions.stem: A 79 year old man has 3 days of poor oral intake. His urea has risen from 6.0 to 28.0 mmol/L while his creatinine has risen from 90 to 150 µmol/L. He has no gastrointestinal bleeding and is not on steroids. His urine osmolality is 710 mOsm/kg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism for the disproportionate rise in urea?
o: Breakdown of blood in the gut
Increased hepatic urea production from steroids
Increased urea reabsorption because tubular flow is slow
questions.e: In pre-renal AKI, slow tubular flow allows more urea to be reabsorbed, so urea rises disproportionately to creatinine; creatinine is filtered and not reabsorbed.

clues: urea has risen from 6.0 to 28.0 mmol/L
steps.x: Pre-renal state: urea rises far more than creatinine with concentrated urine.

elim: There is no GI bleeding.
Would not raise urea.
He is not on steroids.
Causes dilute urine and a proportionate rise.

steps.x: D: Increased urea reabsorption because tubular flow is slow. When tubular flow is slow, more urea is reabsorbed; creatinine is not.

questions.stem: A 33 year old man is admitted after a day of hard work outdoors in a heatwave with little to drink. He is dizzy, his mouth is dry and his pulse rate is 112 bpm. His creatinine has risen from 78 to 140 µmol/L. A urine sample is sent before fluids are given.
questions.q: Which urine results are most likely?
questions.e: In pre-renal AKI, reduced renal blood flow activates RAAS, so the kidney avidly retains sodium and water, producing concentrated urine (over 500 mOsm/kg) with low urinary sodium.

steps.x: Dehydration: pre-renal AKI.

elim: Dilute urine is not expected when the kidney is conserving water.
Dilute urine with high sodium fits ATN.
Fits intrinsic tubular injury.
High urinary sodium would not occur with RAAS activation.

steps.x: D: Osmolality 680 mOsm/kg and sodium 8 mmol/L. RAAS activation makes the kidney hold sodium and water: concentrated urine with low sodium.

questions.stem: A 61 year old woman has acute kidney injury after 5 days of intravenous gentamicin. Her urine sodium is 58 mmol/L, fractional excretion of sodium is 2.9% and urine osmolality is 300 mOsm/kg. A student asks why her urine contains so much sodium.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
o: Injured tubular epithelial cells cannot reabsorb sodium
questions.e: Gentamicin directly injures tubular epithelial cells, which can no longer reabsorb sodium or concentrate urine, so ATN gives a high urinary sodium, FeNa over 1% and dilute urine.

steps.x: Nephrotoxin with high urinary sodium and FeNa over 1%.

elim: Would lower urinary sodium.
Causes proteinuria and haematuria, not mainly sodium loss.
Would not explain dilute urine with tubular injury.
Gentamicin does not cause obstruction.

steps.x: D: Injured tubular epithelial cells cannot reabsorb sodium. ATN: injured tubular cells cannot reabsorb sodium, giving high urinary sodium, high FeNa and dilute urine.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man with prostate cancer has bilateral hydronephrosis and a creatinine of 480 µmol/L. Bilateral nephrostomies are inserted. Over the next 4 days his creatinine falls to 160 µmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism by which the obstruction had reduced his kidney function?
o: Immune complex deposition in the glomeruli
Raised intratubular pressure reducing the glomerular filtration gradient
questions.e: Obstruction raises intratubular and Bowman's capsule pressure, reducing the gradient driving glomerular filtration; relieving it with a nephrostomy or catheter restores flow and GFR.

steps.x: Function recovers once urine can drain.

elim: He has an obstructive cause, not a drug cause.
Glomerulonephritis does not improve with nephrostomies.
The ACE inhibitor mechanism, not obstruction.
The ATN mechanism, which does not recover with drainage.

steps.x: D: Raised intratubular pressure reducing the glomerular filtration gradient. Obstruction raises pressure in the tubules, opposing filtration; relieving it restores flow.

questions.stem: A 72 year old woman with peripheral vascular disease and a renal bruit starts ramipril. Ten days later her creatinine has risen from 105 to 210 µmol/L. Doppler ultrasound shows severe bilateral renal artery stenosis.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of the fall in her GFR?
o: Loss of angiotensin II-mediated efferent arteriolar constriction
questions.e: With renal artery stenosis, glomerular pressure depends on angiotensin II constricting the efferent arteriole; ACE inhibitors reduce efferent tone, so GFR falls and creatinine rises.

steps.x: Renal hypoperfusion from stenosis, then an ACE inhibitor.

elim: Would increase GFR.
An idiosyncratic reaction, not linked to renal artery stenosis.
ACE inhibitors are not directly toxic to tubules.
Not caused by ACE inhibitors.

steps.x: D: Loss of angiotensin II-mediated efferent arteriolar constriction. In stenosis, GFR depends on angiotensin II constricting the efferent arteriole; ACE inhibitors remove it.

questions.stem: A 56 year old man has stage 3 acute kidney injury from acute tubular necrosis. He is breathing deeply. His chest is clear and his lactate is normal. His arterial blood gas results are shown.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his acid-base disturbance?
o: Failure to excrete the daily acid load and regenerate bicarbonate
questions.e: Metabolic acidosis develops in AKI because the kidneys can no longer excrete the daily acid load or regenerate bicarbonate; his lactate is normal, so it is not lactic acidosis.

steps.x: Low pH and bicarbonate with a low CO2 (compensation): metabolic acidosis in AKI.

elim: He has no diarrhoea.
Would cause a respiratory alkalosis.
There is no diabetes or starvation suggested.
His lactate is normal.

steps.x: B: Failure to excrete the daily acid load and regenerate bicarbonate. Failing kidneys cannot excrete acid or regenerate bicarbonate.

questions.stem: A 69 year old woman with acute kidney injury and a potassium of 7.0 mmol/L is given 30 mL of 10% calcium gluconate intravenously. Her ECG tented T waves improve within minutes. A repeat potassium 15 minutes later is still 7.0 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of the calcium gluconate effect?
o: Increasing potassium excretion in the gut
Removing potassium from the blood by dialysis
questions.e: Calcium gluconate stabilises the cardiac myocyte membrane against the depolarising effect of hyperkalaemia, protecting against arrhythmia, but it does not lower serum potassium.

steps.x: ECG improves but potassium is unchanged.

elim: This is how potassium binders work.
This is how loop diuretics work.
This is how insulin and salbutamol work.
Calcium does not remove potassium.

steps.x: A: Cardiac membrane stabilisation. IV calcium gluconate stabilises the myocardium without lowering potassium.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man has oliguric acute kidney injury. Over 3 days, despite no potassium supplements and a low-potassium diet, his potassium rises from 4.6 to 6.4 mmol/L. His urine output is 150 mL per day.
questions.q: Which is the most likely reason his potassium is rising?
o: Increased potassium secretion by the colon
questions.e: The kidney is the main route of potassium excretion, so oliguric AKI leads to hyperkalaemia even without intake; acidosis worsens it by shifting potassium out of cells.

steps.x: Oliguria with steadily rising potassium.

elim: Gut absorption is not the cause.
This would lower potassium.
Possible, but a steady rise over days in oliguric AKI is real.
Shifts potassium into cells, lowering it.

steps.x: A: Failure of renal potassium excretion. The kidney is the principal route of potassium excretion.
